1. Captain Dimitrios Kontos (Δημήτριος Κοντός) and a crew of sponge divers from Symi island discovered the Antikythera wreck in early 1900, and recovered artefacts during the first expedition with the Hellenic Royal Navy, in 1900–1901.
2. This wreck of a Roman cargo ship was found at a depth of 45 metres (148 ft) off Point Glyphadia on the Greek island of Antikythera.
3. The team retrieved numerous large objects, including bronze and marble statues, pottery, unique glassware, jewellery, coins, and the mechanism.
4. The mechanism was retrieved from the wreckage in 1901, probably July.
5. It is unknown how the mechanism came to be on the cargo ship.
6. All of the items retrieved from the wreckage were transferred to the National Museum of Archaeology in Athens for storage and analysis.
7. The mechanism appeared to be a lump of corroded bronze and wood.
8. The bronze had turned into atacamite which cracked and shrank when it was brought up from the shipwreck, changing the dimensions of the pieces.
9. It went unnoticed for two years, while museum staff worked on piecing together more obvious treasures, such as the statues.
10. Upon removal from seawater, the mechanism was not treated, resulting in deformational changes.
11. He initially believed that it was an astronomical clock, but most scholars considered the device to be prochronistic, too complex to have been constructed during the same period as the other pieces that had been discovered.
12. The German philologist Albert Rehm became interested in the device and was the first to propose that it was an astronomical calculator.
